item.content:encoded:
Anthropic mathematician claims AI-assisted proof of Riemann hypothesis

Category: Science

Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at artificial intelligence company Anthropic, said on Nov. 20 that he and the company’s Claude model had proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old conjecture about the distribution of prime numbers. He released a formal proof written in 17 million lines of Lean code, which lets software check mathematical steps [3][10]. The Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib, a volunteer-led mathematics project, said they had “full confidence” in the proof’s soundness and confirmed that its code compiles [3]. The full argument has not yet been explained in a readily understandable form. The machine-checkable proof establishes a result without, by itself, showing researchers why it works or how to build on it [3][16]. Mathematicians are working to digest the proof and extract its ideas. The result does not break RSA encryption, which depends on the difficulty of factoring large numbers, not on proving how prime numbers are distributed [5][14].

Primary Source: View original article

Read more: Full article on Kite Static

I don't think this kind of proof would ever come from a human.

— Abhishek Saha, professor of mathematics at Queen Mary University of London (WIRED)

Did you know: The generalized Riemann hypothesis can help mathematicians determine which numbers can be written as a square plus another square plus seven times a third square [5].

Key Points

  • Proof dissection: More than 60 people were using AI agents to translate sections of the proof, and contributors had produced explanations for over 3,000 segments. One mathematician estimated the work could take months [3].
  • AI research: OpenAI released 722 AI-generated mathematics papers the month before Alpöge’s announcement. Some were later retracted after errors were found [1].
  • Small result: Mathematicians have already extracted one smaller result from Alpöge’s proof and written it up separately [3].

Perspectives

Association for Human Mathematics: The group argued that the announcement prioritizes technical validity over clarity and accountability, and said no person can reasonably claim to understand the document [3][2].

Sources: WIRED

David Manderscheid, mathematician: Manderscheid argues that graduate mathematics programs should ask students not only to solve problems but also to explain and contextualize proofs, since AI can now complete work once assigned to doctoral students [1].

Sources: The Conversation

Cybersecurity experts: Experts urged security teams to inventory cryptographic systems, replace obsolete 1024-bit RSA keys and continue planned migrations to post-quantum standards [14].

Sources: Computerworld

Timeline

  • 1859: Riemann formulated his conjecture about the distribution of prime numbers [10]
  • 2000: The Clay Mathematics Institute named it one of seven Millennium Prize Problems [10]
  • October 2026: OpenAI released 722 AI-generated mathematics papers [1]
  • 21 November 2026: The Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib expressed confidence in the compiled proof [3]

Industry Impact

  • Cryptography: Beyond the Riemann hypothesis, Computerworld reported that Claude Mythos found a mathematical flaw in HAWK, a proposed post-quantum signature standard, and a faster attack on weakened AES; AI agents have also reduced the cost of running existing software on graphics chips [14].

Scientific Significance

  • Mathematical methods: AI systems can draw on tools across mathematical fields, but traditional work on proofs also produces connections, shortcuts and methods that other researchers can reuse [16].
  • Limits of AI-led discovery: So far, AI has tackled problems people already identified as important; there is no evidence it can independently recognize or formulate significant open questions [16].

Historical Background

Riemann used the zeta function to explain discrepancies between Gauss’s estimates of prime counts and the actual counts; if true, the hypothesis would reveal order in that distribution [10]. In 2000, the Clay Mathematics Institute named it one of seven Millennium Prize Problems and offered $1 million for a solution [10][14]. The institute’s prize program was intended to encourage new mathematical ideas, not simply the completion of a list of challenges, according to a September open letter signed by 28 Fields Medal winners [2].

England records 5,258 heat-linked deaths after record-hot summer

Category: Science

England recorded an estimated 5,258 deaths associated with extreme heat between May and September 2026, the highest total since the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) began monitoring in 2016 and nearly twice the previous record of 2,985 in 2022 [6][8]. The figures are provisional because death-registration data for the period are incomplete [6]. The agency counted seven heat episodes lasting a total of 41 days, both records since monitoring began [5][8][6]. The deadliest stretch was June 21-28, when heat was associated with an estimated 2,401 deaths; more than 3,000 deaths were linked to episodes in May and June combined [5][6]. Heat can trigger heatstroke and dehydration or worsen cardiovascular and respiratory conditions [5]. Dr Ross Thompson, UKHSA’s principal environmental health scientist, said periods of extreme heat are expected to become longer, more frequent and more intense as the climate warms [6].

UK Health Security Agency: The agency said heat precautions should begin at the start of summer because people and public services may be less prepared for early-season heat, and urged longer-term adaptation of homes, neighbourhoods and health and care settings [6].

item.content:encoded:
US consumer confidence jumps to 103.3, highest since January 2025

Category: Business

US consumer confidence rose 11.4 points in November to 103.3, its highest level since January 2025, the Conference Board said Tuesday. The increase exceeded forecasts and followed the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Confidence rose sharply among Democrats and independents after the election but edged down among Republicans. Respondents remained frustrated by high prices, while their assessments of jobs and the economy improved [2][3][6]. Reduced post-election uncertainty and falling gasoline prices were cited as possible reasons for the rebound. The national average gasoline price was $3.61 a gallon on Nov. 24, down from $4.30 a month earlier but still above $3.07 a year earlier. October inflation was reported at 4%, up from 3.7% in September [9][7]. Consumer spending had remained robust through two quarters despite weak sentiment, and economists say surveys have become less reliable measures of behavior [2][7]. The Federal Reserve was expected to raise its benchmark rate by a quarter percentage point at its next meeting, about two weeks away, as it continued efforts to curb inflation [6].

Primary Source: View original article

Key Points

  • Current conditions: The Conference Board’s Present Situation Index rose 13.7 points to 132.8, while its Expectations Index gained 9.9 points to 83.6 [15][1].
  • Job perceptions: The share saying jobs were plentiful reached 30.8%, up from 26.2%; those saying jobs were hard to get fell to 18.4% from 21.4% [2].
  • Vacation plans: The share of respondents planning a vacation in the next six months reached 44.9%, up 2.2 percentage points from October, with domestic travel intentions rising and overseas plans falling [1].
  • Uneven gains: Confidence increased across age groups, with the biggest rise among Gen Z respondents; consumers in higher-income households recorded the largest improvement [15][2].
  • Inflation expectations: Consumers’ expectations for inflation over the next 12 months fell for a second consecutive month but remained elevated at 5.7% [6].

Perspectives

Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS, warned that trouble in artificial intelligence stock valuations could slow consumption through the wealth effect [2].

  • 3 November 2026: Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm elections [2][1]
  • 24 November 2026: Conference Board released November confidence index at 103.3 [2][3]

Historical Background

The confidence index rose for a second consecutive month in November after falling in September to its lowest level since April 2014, below its level during the pandemic [7][9].

Q&A

Q: What economic report was due next?

A: The Commerce Department was scheduled to release a separate inflation measure closely watched by the Federal Reserve on Nov. 25 [9][11].

Q: What does the survey say about the kinds of purchases consumers are considering?

A: Respondents reported increased plans to buy motor vehicles, major appliances and homes over the following six months [2].
